docs.title: Scopus
docs.text:
A research analytics platform for collecting faculty publication records and streaming extraction progress to the browser.

Scopus consolidates publication data from Google Scholar and Elsevier Scopus APIs. A FastAPI backend coordinates long-running extraction jobs, checks for reusable generated reports, and exposes progress through Server-Sent Events (SSE). A React interface presents the workflow and makes the resulting datasets available in multiple export formats.

docs.title: What this documentation covers
docs.text:
• The application architecture and its service boundaries.
  • The lifecycle of an asynchronous publication extraction job.
  • Cache-first behavior and upstream API concurrency controls.
  • How progress moves from a background worker to the browser through SSE.
  • Data outputs, API workflows, and operational considerations.

docs.title: At a glance
docs.text: Area Technology / responsibility Backend Python, FastAPI Frontend React 19 Publication sources Google Scholar and Elsevier Scopus APIs Local persistence SQLite Progress delivery Server-Sent Events (SSE) Job execution FastAPI background task workflow Exports CSV, JSON, Excel, PDF Deployment support Docker

docs.title: Core workflow
docs.text:
1. The browser requests a publication extraction job.
  2. The backend checks whether reusable reports already exist.
  3. If extraction is required, the backend starts a background worker and returns without making the browser wait for the entire job.
  4. The worker gathers and consolidates publication records, calculates metrics, and writes output files.
  5. The browser receives live progress events through an SSE connection.
  6. The user downloads the generated reports.

Read the system overview Explore the extraction workflow

docs.title: Integration notes
docs.text:
• Treat the job-start response as an acknowledgement, not proof that extraction has completed.
  • Use the job ID to subscribe to the corresponding progress stream.
  • Handle SSE disconnections and reconnect behavior in the frontend.
  • Use the download routes only after the relevant artifact has been generated.
  • Check the API's current validation rules, response schemas, and error codes before writing client code.

docs.title: High-level design
docs.text:
Scopus separates interactive browser requests from time-consuming academic data collection. FastAPI coordinates the workflow, while a background extraction task performs external network I/O and file generation.

flowchart TD
    U[User] --> UI[React 19 interface]
    UI -->|POST /api/fetch/start| API[FastAPI backend]
    API --> CACHE{Reusable reports?}
    CACHE -->|Yes| ART[Generated reports]
    CACHE -->|No| JOB[Background extraction job]
    JOB --> SCH[Google Scholar]
    JOB --> SC[Elsevier Scopus API]
    SCH --> PROC[Merge, deduplicate and calculate metrics]
    SC --> PROC
    PROC --> DB[(SQLite)]
    PROC --> ART
    JOB --> STORE[In-memory PROGRESS_STORE]
    STORE --> SSE[SSE endpoint]
    SSE -->|progress events| UI
    ART -->|download endpoints| UI

docs.title: React interface
docs.text: The frontend starts an extraction request and subscribes to the job-specific progress stream using the browser's EventSource interface. It also presents generated report downloads.

docs.title: FastAPI application
docs.text: The API layer accepts extraction requests, checks for cached artifacts, creates job identifiers, starts background work, exposes the SSE stream, and serves report downloads.

docs.title: Background extraction worker
docs.text: The worker performs the slow operations: querying external sources, processing pages of results, consolidating records, computing publication metrics, and writing output artifacts.

docs.title: Progress store and SSE endpoint
docs.text: The worker publishes progress state to an in-memory PROGRESS_STORE. The SSE endpoint reads that state and streams updates to the matching browser connection.

docs.title: Storage and generated files
docs.text: SQLite provides lightweight structured persistence. Generated CSV, JSON, Excel, and PDF files are separate downloadable artifacts. The in-memory progress store is transient telemetry, not durable job history.

docs.title: Architectural trade-off
docs.text: Keeping extraction outside the initial request-response cycle improves responsiveness for workflows involving multiple paginated API calls. The trade-off is that job progress is held in process memory; deployments that require durable job recovery or multiple backend workers need a shared progress/job store.

docs.title: Cache-first behavior
docs.text:
Before starting a new extraction, the backend checks whether generated reports are already available. When a reusable result exists and force_refresh=false, the application can serve those artifacts without repeating the same external API work.

This behavior can reduce duplicate upstream requests and make repeat access faster.

docs.title: Force refresh
docs.text: A force-refresh option allows the caller to request a fresh extraction instead of using reusable generated output. The exact request schema and cache invalidation behavior should be checked against the current API implementation before integrating another client.

docs.title: Concurrency guard
docs.text:
Academic data providers enforce usage limits. The documented architecture uses a semaphore-style concurrency guard to control competing extraction activity.

The guard is intended to: - Prevent multiple extraction jobs from saturating upstream API capacity. - Reduce avoidable overlapping requests. - Keep resource-intensive work from accumulating without control.

docs.title: Retry behavior
docs.text: Network calls can fail for transient reasons. The implementation includes request exception handling and retry-related logic in its HTTP helper. Do not assume every HTTP error status is retried: verify the current helper's status-code handling and retry policy before documenting guarantees such as exponential backoff or automatic retry on HTTP 429.

docs.title: Operational guidance
docs.text:
• Prefer cached reports when a refresh is not necessary.
  • Avoid launching repeated jobs for the same author while an extraction is already running.
  • Treat upstream API limits as an external dependency.
  • Log source-specific failures so partial extraction problems can be diagnosed.

docs.title: Source aggregation
docs.text:
Scopus consolidates faculty publication metadata from Google Scholar and Elsevier Scopus APIs. The extraction worker gathers records, merges source results, and prepares structured datasets for downstream reporting.

The exact fields available depend on the upstream source and the metadata returned for each publication. Do not assume that every source provides every citation or bibliographic field.

docs.title: Deduplication and metrics
docs.text:
The documented extraction workflow identifies duplicate records using DOI-based matching. It also computes publication and citation indicators, including:

  • h-index
  • i10-index

These indicators are derived from the collected publication data. Their accuracy depends on source coverage, author identity matching, and the completeness of the retrieved records.

docs.title: Output formats
docs.text: Format Typical use CSV Tabular data processing and spreadsheet import JSON Programmatic integration and structured data exchange Excel Review and analysis in spreadsheet applications PDF Shareable report presentation

docs.title: Persistence
docs.text:
SQLite is used for lightweight local structured persistence. The application also writes generated report artifacts that are served through download endpoints.

Keep the distinction clear: - SQLite stores structured application data. - Generated files are export artifacts. - PROGRESS_STORE holds transient extraction telemetry while jobs run.

docs.title: Publication extraction workflow
docs.text: The extraction lifecycle is divided into three phases: initialization, background processing, and progress delivery.

docs.title: Phase 1: Job initialization and cache interception
docs.text:
1. The React interface sends POST /api/fetch/start with the author identifier and extraction options.
  2. The backend checks the generated-artifact area for reusable reports.
  3. If reports exist and force_refresh=false, the backend can return the cached artifacts rather than repeating upstream API calls.
  4. If fresh extraction is needed, a concurrency guard checks whether another operation is already consuming the available upstream API capacity.

The cache check is intended to avoid unnecessary external requests. The concurrency guard helps prevent overlapping extraction work from placing excessive pressure on vendor APIs.

docs.title: Phase 2: Non-blocking background execution
docs.text:
1. The backend allocates an ephemeral job ID.
  2. It schedules run_extraction_job as background work.
  3. The start endpoint returns an accepted response instead of waiting for all pages and reports to finish.
  4. The worker queries the configured publication sources, merges and deduplicates records, computes citation metrics, and writes structured outputs.

The documented workflow describes an HTTP 202 Accepted response for a newly accepted background job. Clients should use the returned job identifier to follow progress rather than treating the start response as the completed report.

docs.title: Phase 3: Completion and report delivery
docs.text: The worker updates progress as it processes the extraction. Once the job completes, the progress stream communicates the terminal state and the generated report files can be downloaded through the corresponding API routes.

docs.title: Record consolidation
docs.text: The platform combines records obtained from its academic data sources. DOI-based matching is used in the documented workflow to identify duplicate publication records. Where DOI data is unavailable, title normalization may be used by the implementation; confirm the current repository code before relying on a specific fallback rule.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Scopus addresses the manual effort involved in collecting faculty publication records from separate academic portals. It provides a single extraction workflow that gathers records from Google Scholar and Elsevier Scopus APIs, consolidates the results, and generates structured reports.

docs.title: Main application areas
docs.text: Area Responsibility React interface Starts extraction, displays progress, and exposes report downloads FastAPI backend Validates requests, coordinates extraction jobs, serves progress events, and provides downloads Background extraction worker Performs paginated external API requests and processes publication records Generated-artifact cache Allows existing reports to be reused when a refresh is not requested SQLite Lightweight local persistence for structured records External academic APIs Supply publication metadata and citation-related information

docs.title: Typical user journey
docs.text:
1. Open the application and provide the faculty/author identifier required by the interface.
  2. Start extraction.
  3. The backend either returns reusable generated reports or accepts a new background job.
  4. For a new job, keep the progress view open while the browser receives SSE events.
  5. When processing completes, download the available CSV, JSON, Excel, or PDF report.

docs.title: Important distinction
docs.text: The HTTP request that starts a job and the SSE connection that reports progress serve different purposes. The start request initiates work; the SSE connection delivers subsequent status updates. The browser does not need to keep the initial request open for the duration of the extraction.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Term Meaning Academic metadata Bibliographic information describing a publication Background job Work executed after the initiating request has returned Cache-first Checking for reusable generated output before making new upstream requests DOI Digital Object Identifier used to identify scholarly works EventSource Browser API for receiving Server-Sent Events h-index Citation metric balancing publication count and citation impact i10-index Count of publications with at least ten citations Job ID Identifier used to associate progress events with an extraction run Pagination Retrieving a large result set across multiple API pages PROGRESS_STORE In-memory structure used to expose active job progress SSE Server-Sent Events; a one-way server-to-client event stream Upstream API External service from which publication metadata is retrieved

docs.title: Local setup
docs.text:
Clone the project repository:

git clone https://github.com/Armankb2/Scopus.git
cd Scopus

Create and activate a virtual environment:

python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate

Install dependencies using the repository's documented dependency file. For example, if the project provides requirements.txt:

pip install -r requirements.txt

Start the FastAPI application using the entry point and command documented by the repository. The exact module path and port can vary with the checked-out version.

docs.title: Docker
docs.text: The project lists Docker as part of its technology stack. Use the repository's Dockerfile and compose configuration, if present, rather than assuming a container service layout.

docs.title: Operational checks
docs.text:
• Verify that required API credentials are configured through environment variables or the repository's intended secret-management mechanism.
  • Confirm upstream API access and quota availability.
  • Check that the generated-artifact directory is writable.
  • Confirm that SQLite storage is available to the running process.
  • Ensure the frontend can reach the API and establish an SSE connection.
  • Monitor partial failures from individual academic data sources.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Symptom Checks Extraction takes a long time Check upstream latency, pagination, and rate limits Progress is not updating Confirm the job ID and SSE endpoint; inspect backend logs SSE disconnects Check proxy timeout and reconnection behavior Cached report is returned unexpectedly Review the force-refresh option and generated-artifact cache A report download fails Confirm extraction completion and artifact filename/path Publication counts differ between sources Review author matching, source coverage, and deduplication

Note

This guide intentionally avoids inventing a fixed Uvicorn command, port, or Docker Compose service name. Use the current repository configuration for those values.

docs.title: Why SSE is used
docs.text:
Publication extraction can take several minutes because it involves paginated network requests and data processing. A single long-running HTTP request would make the browser wait for the entire operation.

Scopus uses two separate connections:

  • A normal HTTP request to start extraction.
  • A persistent SSE connection to receive progress updates.

SSE is a server-to-client event stream over HTTP. It is suitable for progress telemetry because the browser needs to receive updates from the server, not send a continuous stream of messages back.

docs.title: Event flow
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant UI as React UI
    participant API as FastAPI
    participant Worker as Extraction worker
    participant Store as PROGRESS_STORE
    UI->>API: POST /api/fetch/start
    API->>Worker: Schedule run_extraction_job
    API-->>UI: Accepted response + job ID
    UI->>API: EventSource(/api/progress/{job_id})
    loop While extraction runs
        Worker->>Store: Publish status and percentage
        API-->>UI: SSE progress event
    end
    Worker->>Store: Publish complete state
    API-->>UI: Final SSE event

docs.title: Frontend subscription
docs.text:
The browser uses the job identifier returned by the start request to open an EventSource connection to:

GET /api/progress/{job_id}

The browser receives updates as they are emitted by the backend. This avoids repeatedly requesting the progress endpoint with timer-based polling.

docs.title: In-memory progress state
docs.text:
PROGRESS_STORE holds transient job progress information for the SSE endpoint. It is useful for communicating the current state while the process is running, but it should not be confused with SQLite records or generated report files.

Deployment consideration

In-memory progress state is tied to the running application process. A process restart can lose that state, and separate workers may not share it. A multi-instance production deployment should use shared state or a durable job system if cross-process progress continuity is required.

docs.title: Why these components fit
docs.text:
• FastAPI provides an API layer for coordinating requests and background work.
  • Background tasks separate long-running extraction from the initial browser request.
  • SSE provides a simple one-way progress channel to the React interface.
  • SQLite keeps local persistence lightweight for a self-contained research analytics application.
  • Multiple export formats support both programmatic use and human review.
